title: Flatten a Multilevel Doubly Linked List
statement:
You get `head`, the first node of the top level of a multilevel doubly linked list. Each node has an integer `val`, links `prev` and `next` to its neighbours within its own level, and a link `child` that is either `null` or the first node of another doubly linked list one level lower, whose nodes may have children of their own. Relink the nodes into one single-level doubly linked list: whenever a node has a child list, that whole list (itself flattened) must come directly after the node and before the node's original `next`. When you finish, every `child` is `null` and every `prev` points to the node just before it (`null` for the first node). Reuse the original nodes and return the head of the flattened list, or `null` when the list is empty.

Each case is written as `[head]`, the structure serialized row by row. The first row is the top level's values. Every later row is the child list of one node in the row just before it, and is written as a `null` that closes the previous row, then one `null` for each node of the previous row that comes before its owner (so no extra `null` means the first node owns it), then the row's values; trailing `null`s are left out. Your function receives the top level's first node, and the result is shown as the flattened list's values from head to tail. (The TypeScript starter types nodes as `_Node`, which does not list `prev` and `child`; the objects still have both.)
constraints: The list has between 0 and 1000 nodes
notes:
## Intuition

A brute force walks the structure depth first (a node, then its child list, then its `next`), stores the nodes in that order and relinks them all, which costs O(n) extra space. You can instead splice in place: when the walk reaches a node with a child, the child list must sit between that node and its old `next`. Only the child's own level has to be inserted at that moment; its deeper children are met and spliced later, because the walk continues straight into the inserted list.

## Approach

1. Walk the list with `node`, starting at `head`.
2. When `node.child` is set, call it `child` and move `tail` to the last node of that child level.
3. Hook `tail` to `node.next` (and point that node's `prev` back at `tail` when it exists).
4. Make `child` the new `node.next`, set `child.prev = node`, and clear `node.child`.
5. Step to `node.next`, which now enters the spliced list, and repeat until the end. Return `head`.

## Example 1, step by step

- Nodes `1` and `2` have no child. At `3`, `child = 7` and `tail` runs `7 → 8 → 9 → 10`. Linking `10 ↔ 4` and `3 ↔ 7` gives `1 2 3 7 8 9 10 4 5 6`.
- The walk enters `7`, then `8`, whose child is `11`; `tail` stops at `12`. Linking `12 ↔ 9` and `8 ↔ 11` gives `1 2 3 7 8 11 12 9 10 4 5 6`.
- No other node has a child, so that order is returned.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): each level is scanned once to find its tail and once more by the main walk.
- Space: O(1): only a few pointers are used.

## Pitfalls

- Clear `node.child` after splicing; the judge rejects any node that still has a child.
- Fix the `prev` links on both seams, `child.prev` and the old next's `prev`, not just the `next` links.
- The old `node.next` may be `null` (the child hangs from a level's last node); guard before touching its `prev`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `node` | current node of the walk |
| `child` | first node of the child level being spliced in |
| `tail` | last node of that child level |

narration.2: Start the walk at the head of the top level.
narration.3: Keep walking until the end of the (growing) flattened list.
narration.4: Does this node have a child list to splice in?
narration.5: Remember the first node of the child level.
narration.6: tail will find the last node of that level.
narration.7: Advance while the child level continues.
narration.10: Hook the child level's last node to whatever followed the current node.
narration.11: Was there a node after the current one?
narration.12: Then point its prev back at the tail of the child level.
narration.14: The child level now comes right after the current node.
narration.15: Link the child's prev back to the current node.
narration.16: Clear the child link; the level is now part of the single list.
narration.18: Move on; this enters the spliced child level, so deeper children are handled next.
narration.20: Every level has been spliced in; return the original head.
